name: Grape wine making, Kvemo Kartli, Georgia
summary: Residues in jars at two villages in Kvemo Kartli are interpreted as evidence of grape wine, ca. 6000–5800 BCE.
description: McGovern and colleagues interpret tartaric and other acids in Neolithic jar sherds from Gadachrili Gora and Shulaveris Gora as evidence of grape wine, considering grape pollen and local growing conditions. The jars may have served for fermenting, storing or serving a grape product. Their residues alone cannot establish fermentation, grape domestication or the use of each vessel.

impact.note: Reach 1 because the paper says priority among Near Eastern regions cannot be assigned, so the descent of later wine cultures from these villages is unproven and only the South Caucasus is counted; wine was a new storable drink and substance of ritual and exchange (depth 2); a few direct successors in regional viniculture (generativity 1).

date.label: ca. 6000–5800 BC
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: The excavators and chemical analysts interpret residues in early Neolithic jars from Gadachrili Gora and Shulaveris Gora as evidence of likely grape wine at about 6000–5800 BCE.

evidence.locator: Archaeological Samples Chosen for Analysis, Pottery Prerequisites, Results and Discussion
evidence.supports: Reports organic acid detections compared with controls and attributes the jar residues to grape wine in view of local archaeological and environmental evidence.
Shows why tartaric acid alone cannot identify wine or its production.

earliest_record.rationale: The earliest dated evidence found for this capability in this community. No review has yet confirmed that nothing earlier exists.

unresolved.note: Hajji Firuz Tepe in Iran, whose wine jars the paper places half a millennium later, and the Areni-1 winery in Armenia were not researched and may deserve their own records.
Whether the grapes were cultivated or wild: the sites lie within the range of the wild Eurasian grape, and the paper calls for more excavation and DNA analysis of wild vines.
The place is the province; the two villages lie within 2 km of each other about 50 km south of Tbilisi, and their exact coordinates were not taken from a gazetteer.

Joint position in broad Near Eastern ceramic history does not identify a source for the local jars. Compare paste, forming traces and dated series from the South Caucasus and neighbouring regions. Residue samples support vessel contact and cannot isolate the production step.

research.note: Asked which region has priority in the discovery and spread of the wine culture and the domesticated grape, the authors answer that 'It is impossible to assign priority to any of these regions at this stage in the investigation', so neither independence nor derivation is established.

caveats: The sampled pottery supports contact with a likely grape product. Whether a jar fermented, stored or served it is unresolved. The earliest evidence does not establish domesticated grapes or a line of transmission to later wine regions.
